deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (my interpretation, consistent with this page and the next). Write
  B = -cos a sin b/(cos phi cos delta) = sin h sin e,
  C = (sin a cos b - sin phi sin delta)/(cos phi cos delta) = cos h cos e
(both are on folio 32). With H1 = a+b and H2 = a-b, sin H1 + sin H2 = 2 sin a cos b and sin H1 - sin H2 = 2 cos a sin b. Also cos(h-e) + cos(h+e) = 2 cos h cos e and cos(h-e) - cos(h+e) = 2 sin h sin e. So B and C are exactly the half-sum and half-difference of the two altitude equations
  sin H1 = sin phi sin delta + cos phi cos delta cos(h+e),
  sin H2 = sin phi sin delta + cos phi cos delta cos(h-e).
The setting is therefore the classical two-altitude problem: two altitudes of one star (declination delta, latitude phi) taken at hour angles h+-e, with e half the elapsed interval.

On folio 32 Gauss puts x = cos h and y = cos e, with x = A y, xy = C and (1-x^2)(1-y^2) = B^2. Eliminating x and y gives (A-C)(1-AC) = A B^2. With A = tan delta/tan phi (i.e. cos h tan phi = tan delta cos e), A-C and 1/A-C become (sin delta/sin phi - sin a cos b)/(cos phi cos delta) and (sin phi/sin delta - sin a cos b)/(cos phi cos delta). The condition then reduces to p + 1/p = q + 1/q, i.e. (p-q)(pq-1) = 0, with p = sin a/cos b and q = sin delta/sin phi.

THIS PAGE works out the branch p = q.
(1) sin delta = sin phi sin a/cos b. This is the branch p = q.
(2) Gauss first writes cos h tan phi = cos delta cos e cos b/(sin phi sin a). Using (1), this equals cos e/tan delta, which inverts the intended relation cos h tan phi = tan delta cos e.
(3) He solves (2) for cos delta, cos delta = cos h tan phi sin phi sin a/(cos e cos b), and puts it into cos a sin b = cos phi cos delta sin h sin e (sign of B dropped).
(4) Multiplying by cos b/cos a gives cos b sin b = sin^2 phi tan e tan a sin h cos h. This is algebraically consistent with (3).
(5) He expands sin a cos b = sin phi sin delta + cos phi cos delta cos h cos e = sin^2 phi sin a/cos b + cos phi cos delta cos h cos e.
(6) He first substitutes the inverted cos delta, giving + cos phi cos^2 h tan phi sin phi sin a/cos b = sin^2 phi cos^2 h sin a/cos b. Both lines are CROSSED OUT.
(7) He replaces this with the correct substitution cos h = tan delta cos e/tan phi: cos phi cos delta tan delta cos^2 e/tan phi = cos^2 phi (sin delta/sin phi) cos^2 e. By (1) this is cos^2 phi cos^2 e sin a/cos b.
(8) So sin a cos b = (sin a/cos b)(sin^2 phi + cos^2 phi cos^2 e), written as sin a/cos b + cos^2 phi cos^2 e sin a/cos b - cos^2 phi sin a/cos b.
(9) Cancelling sin a/cos b: cos^2 b = 1 - cos^2 phi sin^2 e. Hence sin^2 b = cos^2 phi sin^2 e and +-sin b = cos phi sin e. The 'theta' in the transcription is most likely e. Folio 32 indeed has sin e cos phi = sin b.
(10) Summary line: 1 = sin phi sin a/(cos b sin delta) = tan delta cos e/(cos h tan phi) = cos phi sin a cos e/(cos b cos delta cos h). These are three equivalent forms of the branch conditions. Given (1), the second and third are identical. The marginal cos phi sin a cos e/(cos b cos delta) is the resulting expression for cos h.
(11) Upside-down fragments (lower right): attempts to combine sin e/sin h with cos a cos b, cos delta cos phi/(cos a cos b), tan delta/(cos h tan phi), ending in 'sin e (cos h - 1) = ...'. They are too uncertain to reconstruct reliably. Probably further consequences of the same branch, e.g. using -cos a = cos delta sin h, which follows from B together with sin b = cos phi sin e.
errors: Line 2, cos h tan phi = cos delta cos e cos b/(sin phi sin a), is the reciprocal form. Given sin delta = sin phi sin a/cos b it says cos h tan phi tan delta = cos e, not cos h tan phi = tan delta cos e as in the '1 = ...' line and folio 32 (A = tan delta/tan phi).

Lines 3-4 inherit the inverted relation (cos delta = cos h tan phi sin phi sin a/(cos e cos b)). Line 3 also drops the minus sign in cos a sin b = -cos phi cos delta sin h sin e. Gauss did not cross these lines out but abandoned them.

Gauss himself caught the slip in the expansion of sin a cos b: the two terms built on the inverted substitution are crossed out and replaced by the correct cos phi cos delta tan delta cos^2 e/tan phi.
After correction, the derivation sin^2 b = cos^2 phi sin^2 e is correct.
The upside-down fragments are too unclear to check; no judgement possible.

results.what: Decomposition of the two-altitude equations (same star, hour angles h+-e) into half-sum/half-difference form: sin a cos b = sin phi sin delta + cos phi cos delta cos h cos e and cos a sin b = -cos phi cos delta sin h sin e, with a, b the half-sum and half-difference of the altitudes
results.modern_name: Two-altitude (Douwes) problem: latitude and time from two altitudes and the elapsed interval
results.usually_credited_to: Cornelis Douwes (c. 1740s-1750s); later Pemberton, Lalande, Delambre and others

results.what: Under the auxiliary condition cos h/cos e = tan delta/tan phi, the elimination factors as (p-q)(pq-1) = 0 with p = sin a/cos b and q = sin delta/sin phi. On the branch p = q it follows that sin b = +-cos phi sin e.
results.modern_name: Special/degenerate case analysis of the two-altitude problem (elementary spherical trigonometry)

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary spherical-astronomy algebra on a classical navigation problem that Gauss is known to have worked on (e.g. determining latitude and time from altitudes, Monatliche Correspondenz 1808-09). It is a worked special case with a self-corrected slip; nothing here anticipates later results.

checkable.asserts: Half-sum of the two altitude equations gives the C relation (=0).
Half-difference gives cos a sin b = -cos phi cos delta sin h sin e (=0).

With sin delta = s and cos h = tan delta cos e/tan phi, the right side of the C relation equals (sin a/cos b)(1 - cos^2 phi sin^2 e). Setting this equal to sin a cos b gives sin^2 b = cos^2 phi sin^2 e (=0).
Line 2's right side equals cos e/tan delta, the reciprocal of the intended tan delta cos e (=0).
From x=A*y and x*y=C (x^2=A*C, y^2=C/A), (1-x^2)(1-y^2)=B^2 is equivalent to (A-C)(1-AC)=A*B^2 (=0).
Factorisation p+1/p = q+1/q iff (p-q)(pq-1)=0 used on folio 32 (=0).

checkable.sympy: phi,a,b,e=symbols('phi a b e'); d_=asin(sin(phi)*sin(a)/cos(b)); simplify(tan(d_)*cos(e)/tan(phi) - cos(phi)*sin(a)*cos(e)/(cos(b)*cos(d_)))
checkable.asserts: Given sin delta = sin phi sin a/cos b, the two expressions for cos h in the '1 = ...' line coincide (=0).

transcription_corrections: 'pm sin b = cos phi sin theta': the last symbol is very likely 'e' (sin e), matching folio 32 'sin e cos phi = sin b'.
In line 3 the denominator is 'cos e cos b' with the 'cos b' overwritten/corrected, not a clean deletion.

In the expansion the trailing term reads '- cos phi^2 sin a/cos b' (from sin^2 phi = 1 - cos^2 phi). The 'cos e^2' belongs to the preceding '+ cos^2 phi ... cos e^2 sin a/cos b' term; in that term 'sin delta/sin phi' is cancelled (struck) against sin a/cos b.
'sin b^2 = cos phi^2 sin e^2' (squares written as sin b^2 etc.) is correct as transcribed.
Upside-down lines: readings are highly uncertain; the first symbol of the last line is probably 'sin e' rather than 'sec'.
